data_section_full_text:
We use two samples to test the study’s hypothesis and these are summarized in Table 1.
The first sample is termed the full sample and is drawn from the period 2003–2008 from
the Audit Analytics population (using the COMPUSTAT fiscal year convention). <sup>4</sup> The
analysis of this sample is limited to a set of variables available in the Audit Analytics
database in order to maximize sample size, in particular the inclusion of smaller firms
which are excluded from COMPUSTAT. We restrict the sample to U.S. clients of U.S.
Big 4 practice offices, and for restatement firms the auditor/office identification is based on
the auditor of record when the restated financial statements were originally issued. We
exclude foreign filers and limit the full sample only to those observations for which we can
determine the engagement office, and those observations which have the necessary (nonmissing) data for the control variables: industry classification, client size (total assets), loss
(negative net income), auditor, audit fees, and nonaudit fees. These screens result in a Big
4 client sample of 23,190 firm-year observations, of which 2,557 firm-year observations
(11.1 percent of the sample) have subsequent restatements.

The second sample is a subset of the full sample and is termed the reduced sample.
It includes only those firm-year observations which have additional required data in
COMPUSTAT and CRSP for an expanded set of control variables in the model estimations.
The reduced sample has 17,842 firm-year observations audited by Big 4 offices, of which
2,373 firm-year observations (13.3 percent of the sample) have subsequent restatements.
Accounting restatements are identified using the Audit Analytics Restatements database as of October 20, 2011. <sup>5</sup> We cut off the sample at fiscal year 2008 in order to allow
sufficient time for the subsequent restatements to occur after the original release date of
the financial statements. Cheffers, Whalen, and Usvyatsky (2011) document the average
time lag between the original financial statement release and a subsequent restatement is
about 700 days, or roughly two years. Therefore, cutting off the sample in 2008 provides
sufficient time to pass so that we are confident of correctly classifying restating and nonrestating companies. Importantly, Audit Analytics indicates the year the restated financial

4. Audit Analytics data is converted to COMPUSTAT fiscal year convention (i.e., when a company’s fiscal
year ends between January 1 and May 31, the previous year is used to denote its fiscal year). Further, in
selecting the sample from Audit Analytics it is important that one does not use only restatements that are
denoted “adverse” by Audit Analytics, which is defined as restatements having an adverse effect on the
financial statements. Using only “adverse” restatements screens out income-increasing restatements and
restatements with no income effects.
5. Note that there are nonaccounting reasons for restatements such restatements arising from mergers and acquisitions. However, all restatements in Audit Analytics are accounting-related and are classified by Audit Analytics into five (overlapping) categories: (1) accounting rule (GAAP) application failures; (2) financial fraud,

irregularities, and misrepresentations; (3) accounting and clerical application errors; (4) regulatory investigations; and (5) other significant issues. Other significant issues contain, but are not limited to, auditor-related
issues, asset retirement issues, deferred/stock-based/executive compensation issues, GAAP changes, revenue
recognition issues, loan covenant violations, and internal control issues. We use all available restatements in
the Audit Analytics Restatement database. For the reduced sample there are 2,373 restatements in total, all of
which are due to accounting rule (GAAP) application failures. In addition, 41 of these restatements are also
classified as being due to fraud, 295 due to regulatory investigations, 251 are classified as other significant
issues, and none in the sample is classified as a clerical application error. As a sensitivity analysis, we also
examine separately just those restatements relating to fraud, regulatory investigations, and other significant
issues, similar to Table 4 using the reduced sample with additional firm-level control variables. The coefficient
on the test variable, OFFICE is negative and significant at p < 0.01, so the study’s results reported in Table 4
using all restatements are consistent with a smaller subsample (525) of the most serious restatements.
